1.pericope_label: After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward

schools.summary: Calvin asks why a vision was needed at all when Abram's affairs were prosperous and the Lord speaks to him here as to one sorrowful and afflicted with fear. Certain writers conjecture that on returning from the deliverance of his nephew he was subjected to some annoyance of which Moses makes no mention, just as the Lord often humbles his people lest they exult in their prosperity; but since the words of Moses give no warrant for the conjecture, Calvin thinks the cause different. Although Abram was on all sides applauded, various surmises entered his own mind: Chedorlaomer and his allies had been overcome, yet he had so provoked them that they might with fresh troops attack the land again, nor were the inhabitants free from that fear. Signal success commonly draws envy along with it, so that Abram, having dared to enter into conflict with an army that had conquered four kings, became formidable and an object of suspicion, and an unfavourable surmise might arise that he would by and by turn against his neighbours the strength he had tried against foreign kings. There might also be a contrary fault to correct, for it was possible that Abram should be so elated with victory as to forget his calling and seek the acquisition of dominion for himself, wearied as he was with a wandering life; and God anticipates that danger, recalling to his memory the spiritual grace vouchsafed to him, that he might despise all other things. On the promise itself Calvin observes that though it comes last in the text it has precedence in order, since the security God urges has no foundation unless by faith we understand that he cares for us; the causal particle should therefore be inserted, fear not, because I am thy shield. By that word he signifies that Abram would always be safe under his protection, and we ought to regard the promise as a brazen wall, that we should not be excessively fearful in any dangers; in calling himself a reward he teaches Abram to be satisfied with himself alone, and not simply a reward but an exceeding great one, with which we ought to be more than sufficiently contented. Not that the faithful can be entirely free from fear and care while they are tossed by the tempests of contention and misery, but the storm is hushed in their own breast, and faith triumphs over fear. Gill supplies what the opening words point back to: the battle of the kings, the captivity of Lot, the rescue of him and the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the conversation which passed between Abram and the kings of Sodom and Salem.

Clarke notes that this is the first place where God is represented as revealing himself by his word, and reports that some learned men suppose the Hebrew phrase to mean the same as the Logos of John, since the Chaldee paraphrases render it "my word" and appear always to consider it a person, distinguishing it from a term signifying merely a word spoken. He then sets out five ways in which God has revealed his will, not only to the patriarchs but to the prophets and apostles: by a personal appearance of him who was afterwards incarnated for the salvation of mankind; by an audible voice, sometimes accompanied with emblematical appearances; by visions taking place either in the night in ordinary sleep, or when the persons were cast into a temporary trance by daylight; by the ministry of angels appearing in human bodies; and by the powerful agency of the Spirit of God upon the mind, giving it a strong conception and supernatural persuasion of the truth. He judges it probable that the revelation in the text was given in the third of these ways, since the word used comes from a root meaning to see, or according to others to fix or settle, whence the Seer is named — the person to whom divine things are revealed, on whose mind they are fastened, and in whose memory and judgment they are fixed. On the promise Clarke asks whether Abram can be supposed to have understood it of temporal advantage. If he did, he was disappointed through the whole course of his life, for he never enjoyed such worldly prosperity as could justify so strong a promise; nor did the Israelites ever enjoy such affluence as the words seem to intend. What then is meant is just what the words state: God was Abram's portion, and is the portion of every righteous soul, for to Abram and the children of his faith he gives not a portion in this life. Clarke cites Calmet, that nothing proves more invincibly the immortality of the soul and the truth of religion than to see that in this life the righteous seldom receive the reward of their virtue. The exceeding great reward is not the Canaan promised but the salvation to come through the promised seed, and hence, he says, Abram rejoiced to see the day of Christ, and hence the Chaldee Targum renders the clause, My Word shall be thy strength. Wesley abridges Henry closely, that Abram might fear lest the four kings he had routed should rally and fall upon him, and that God bids him fear neither their revenge nor his neighbour's envy.

Henry takes the occasion, the manner and the substance of the promise in turn. As to the time, it came after that famous act of generous charity in which Abram had rescued his friends and neighbours out of distress, and that not for price nor reward — those that show favour to men shall find favour with God; and it came after the victory over four kings, lest Abram should be too much elevated and pleased with it, God coming to tell him he had better things in store, since a believing converse with spiritual blessings is an excellent means to keep us from being too much taken up with temporal enjoyments, and the gifts of common providence are not comparable to those of covenant love. As to the manner, the word of the Lord came to him in a vision, which supposes Abram awake and some visible appearance of the divine glory, the methods of revelation being adapted to our state in a world of sense. As to the substance, Henry finds three assurances. God called him by name, which was a great honour and also a great encouragement to his faith, for God's good word does us good when it is spoken by his Spirit to us in particular. God cautioned him against being disquieted: Abram might fear lest the four kings he had routed should rally and fall upon him to his ruin, but where there is great faith there may yet be many fears, and God takes cognizance of his people's fears though ever so secret. And God assured him of safety and happiness — as safe as God himself could keep him, since the words are more emphatically rendered I am a shield to thee, present with thee, actually caring for thee, a shield ready to them and a shield round about them; and as happy as God himself could make him, since he says not only that he will reward him but that he will be his reward. Abram had generously refused the rewards which the king of Sodom offered him, and here God comes and tells him he shall be no loser by it; the rewards of believing obedience and self-denial are exceedingly great, and God himself is the chosen and promised felicity of holy souls, chosen in this world and promised in a better.

Keil and Delitzsch treat this as a new revelation differing from the previous ones in form and substance, and constituting a new turning point in Abram's life. The word of Jehovah came to him in a vision, that is, neither by a direct internal address, nor by such a manifestation of himself as fell upon the outward senses, nor in a dream of the night, but in a state of ecstasy by an inward spiritual intuition, and that in the day-time rather than at night. The expression applies to the whole chapter: there is no pause anywhere, nor any sign that the vision ceased or that the action was transferred to the sphere of the senses and of external reality, so that the whole process is to be regarded as an internal one, embracing the opening verses and the request for a sign alike, with this difference only, that from the twelfth verse onwards the ecstasy assumed the form of a prophetic sleep produced by God. Ellicott dates the revelation differently, holding that it was made by night, though not in a dream but in a trance, in which the senses of Abram were closed to all earthly impressions and he became passive in the hands of the Almighty. He notes that the phrase used so constantly afterwards to signify revelation occurs here for the first time, and explains why more formal assurances were now needed. Up to this time Abram had received only general promises of offspring and of the land being the possession of his seed, but years were passing by and the fulfilment of his hopes remained as distant as ever. By the war with the Elamite king he had also made for himself powerful enemies, and though the immediate result was fortunate, many Canaanite nations may have witnessed with displeasure so remarkable an exhibition of the power and energy of an immigrant. And thus the time had come when the patriarch needed and obtained more formal assurances, first of the bestowal upon him of offspring, and secondly of the future possession of Palestine.

2.pericope_label: Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus? To me thou hast given no seed

schools.summary: Henry makes Abram's repeated complaint the occasion of the whole promise that follows. The great affliction that sat heavy upon him was the want of a child, and the complaint of it he pours out before the Lord: though we must never complain of God, we have leave to complain to him, and to be large and particular in the statement of our grievances, since it is some ease to a burdened spirit to open its case to a faithful and compassionate friend, whose ear is always open. The complaint is fourfold. That he had no child — not only no son but no seed, for if he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messiah might have come; and he lays an emphasis on the words to me, since his neighbours were full of children and his servants had children born in his house, so that those who are written childless must see God writing them so, and God often withholds those temporal comforts from his own children which he gives plentifully to strangers. That he was never likely to have any, going down the hill apace, going the way of all the earth, leaving the world and leaving no child behind him. That his servants were, and were likely to remain, to him instead of sons: the steward of his house was faithful, but only as a servant, not as a son, and when he died one born in his house would bear rule over all that for which he had laboured. And that the want of a son took away the comfort of all his enjoyments — all is nothing to me, if I have not a son. Henry then weighs the fault in it. If Abram looked no further than a temporal comfort, the complaint was culpable, and it did ill become the father of the faithful to say, what wilt thou give me, immediately after God had said, I am thy shield and thy exceeding great reward; those do not rightly value their covenant-relation to God who do not think it sufficient to balance the want of any creature-comfort. But if he had an eye to the promised seed, the importunity of his desire was very commendable, since he had wealth and victory and honour, and yet, while kept in the dark about the main matter, all was nothing to him: till we have some comfortable evidence of our interest in Christ we should not rest satisfied with anything else. Yet thus far it was culpable, that there was some diffidence of the promise at the bottom of it, and a weariness of waiting God's time; true believers sometimes find it hard to reconcile God's promises with his providences when they seem to disagree.

Gill makes the complaint turn wholly on the promised seed. What signifies what thou givest me of temporal blessings, if thou withholdest the blessing of a child, from whom it might be hoped and believed would spring the promised Messiah, in whom all nations of the earth shall be blessed? All his wealth and riches, victories and honours are of no avail while he is deprived of this favour, and being advanced in years and going the way of all the earth, what pleasure can he take in them when he has none to inherit them? He notes that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem paraphrase the phrase of going as departing out of the world; and at the third verse he adds that God had bestowed many temporal and spiritual blessings on Abram, having given himself in covenant and all things in it, but had not given him a child. Calvin begins with the divine name, inferring from it that some special mark of divine glory was stamped upon the vision, so that Abram had no doubt respecting its author. Since Satan is a wonderful adept at deceiving, and deludes men with many wiles in the name of God, it was necessary that some sure and notable distinction should appear in true and heavenly oracles, which would not suffer the minds of the holy fathers to waver; not that God appeared as he really is, but so far as he might be comprehended by the human mind. Calvin then grants that Abram, in overlooking a promise so glorious, complaining that he is childless, and murmuring against God, seems to conduct himself with little modesty; what was more desirable than to be received under God's protection and to be happy in the enjoyment of him? Yet the liberty he took admits of excuse, first because the Lord permits us to pour into his bosom those cares by which we are tormented and those troubles with which we are oppressed; and secondly because of the design of the complaint, for he does not simply declare that he is solitary, but, seeing that the effect of all the promises depended upon his seed, he does not improperly require that a pledge so necessary should be given him. If the benediction and salvation of the world was not to be hoped for except through his seed, it is not to be wondered at that other things should vanish from his sight when that principal point seemed to fail; and this is the very reason why God not only regards the complaint of his servant with favour, but immediately gives a propitious answer. Of the heir Calvin says the language is metaphorical, our life being like a race: Abram, of advanced age, says he has so far proceeded that little of his course remains, and adds, to aggravate the indignity, that a foreigner would be his heir. He himself renders the rare Hebrew word as the son of the deserted house, since it was proof of a barren house that the inheritance devolved upon a stranger who would occupy the empty and deserted place.

Clarke begins from the culture rather than the text: the anxiety of the Asiatics to have offspring is intense and universal, and among the Hindoos the want of children renders all other blessings of no esteem. Abram, understanding the promise as relating to that person who was to spring from his family, in whom all the nations of the earth should be blessed, expresses his surprise that there should be such a promise and yet he is about to die childless — for, far from a spiritual seed, he has not even a person in his family who has a natural right to his property, and a stranger is likely to be his heir. On the name of that stranger Clarke reports that commentators are not agreed, and calls the Septuagint's translation at least curious: it takes the rare Hebrew word, which our version renders steward, to have been the name of a female slave born in the household, of whom Eliezer was born, and who on account of the country either of his father or of his mother was called a Damascene. Clarke thinks it extremely probable that our Lord had this passage in view in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, since from Eliezer, by leaving out the first letter, Liezer is formed, which makes Lazarus in the New Testament — the person who from an abject and distressed state was raised to lie in the bosom of Abraham. Wesley presses the emphasis on the word seed: not only no son, but no seed; if he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messiah might have come, who was to be the seed of the woman, but he had neither son nor daughter.

Ellicott begins with the divine title, which is not Jehovah Elohim but Lord Jehovah, "Lord" being the ordinary term of respect; usually the sacred name takes the vowels of the word for lord, but as the two occur here together it takes those of Elohim instead, whence the rendering of our version, in obedience to a Jewish scruple. He hears a slight tone of complaint in the question: Jehovah had promised Abram a reward great exceedingly, and Abram answers that no reward can really be great so long as he has no heir. The clause rendered I go childless he would take either as I am going to my grave childless, or better as I continue to be, and pass my days, in childlessness. On the disputed noun he explains that it is generally taken to mean the son of possession, that is, the possessor or owner of the house when Abram dies, while other authorities derive it from a verb signifying to run about, as if it were Eliezer's business to go to and fro in execution of Abram's orders. The term is rare, and Ellicott judges it to have been chosen for the play of words upon the name of Damascus, which may also explain the odd construction of the last clause, where the Hebrew has literally "he is Damascus Eliezer" rather than the grammatical "he is the Damascene Eliezer," the assonance being spoiled by the correct form. Of the following verse he is blunt: the rendering one born in my house is a mistake, since those born in Abram's house were his servants, whereas the Hebrew is the son of my house — not born of Abram, but the chief of the household next to himself, and its representative. Eliezer was probably born at Damascus.

4.pericope_label: He that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir; look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them

schools.summary: Calvin infers from the answer that God had approved the wish of Abram, and that Abram therefore had not been impelled by any carnal affection to offer up this prayer, but by a pious and holy desire of enjoying the benediction promised to him; for God not only promises him a seed, but a great people, who in number should equal the stars of heaven. Those who expound the passage allegorically, implying that a heavenly seed was promised which might be compared with the stars, may enjoy their own opinion, but Calvin maintains what he thinks more solid, that the faith of Abram was increased by the sight of the stars themselves. For the Lord, in order more deeply to affect his own people and more efficaciously to penetrate their minds, after he has reached their ears by his word also arrests their eyes by external symbols, that eyes and ears may consent together. The sight was therefore not superfluous: God intended to strike the mind of Abram with this thought, that he who by his word alone suddenly produced a host so numerous, by which he might adorn the previously vast and desolate heaven, should surely be able to replenish a desolate house with offspring. Calvin adds that it is not necessary to imagine a nocturnal vision merely because the stars which escape our sight by day would then appear, since the whole was transacted in vision, and Abram had a wonderful scene set before him which would manifestly reveal hidden things to him; though he perhaps might not move a step, it was yet possible for him in vision to be led forth out of his tent. On the question what seed is meant, he answers that neither the posterity of Ishmael nor of Esau is to be taken into the account, since the legitimate seed is reckoned by the promise, which God determined should remain in Isaac and Jacob; and the same doubt arises respecting the posterity of Jacob, because many who could trace their descent from him after the flesh cut themselves off as degenerate sons and aliens from the faith of their fathers. The term is extended indiscriminately to the whole people whom God has adopted to himself, but since many were alienated by their unbelief, we must come for information to Christ, who alone distinguishes true and genuine sons from such as are illegitimate; and in Christ the Gentiles also are gathered together and by faith ingrafted into the body of Abram, so as to have a place among his legitimate sons. Gill notes only that the word came again, either the vision having disappeared and come a second time, or God again speaking to him; and of the leading forth he says it was out of the tent into the open air, done at God's call and direction, or by an impulse upon the mind, or else not real and local at all, but only vision.

Clarke reads the leading forth as a distinct act following the first vision, and it appears to him that the whole transaction took place in the evening. Abram, he suggests, had either two visions, the one recorded at the opening of the chapter and the other at the deep sleep, or else what is mentioned at the beginning is part of what took place after the sacrifice; but he thinks it more likely that there was a vision of the kind already described, and afterwards a second, in which the revelation about the years of bondage was received. After the first, Abram is brought forth abroad to see whether he can number the stars; and as he finds this impossible, he is assured that as they are to him innumerable, so shall his posterity be, and that all should spring from one who should proceed from his own bowels, one who should be his own legitimate child. Wesley, following Henry, makes the hour early in the morning rather than the evening, and reads the comparison in two ways. The seed shall be so numerous, for so the stars seem to a common eye: Abram feared he should have no child at all, and God assures him that his descendants should be so many as not to be numbered. And it shall be so illustrious, resembling the stars in splendour, for to them pertained the glory; Abram's seed according to the flesh were like the dust of the earth, but his spiritual seed are like the stars of heaven, not only numerous but glorious, and very precious.

Ellicott refuses to reduce the leading forth to a figure of speech. There is no reason, he says, for regarding this as a poetical description of a merely mental emotion: with his senses dormant, but alive to every spiritual impression, Abram feels himself led forth from the tent into the open space around, and is there commanded to count the stars. On the comparison itself he makes an observation of fact against the usual impression. The stars visible to the naked eye are not in fact very numerous, but they have ever been a received metaphor for an infinite multitude, probably because, as men gaze, they perpetually see the faint radiance of more and more distant constellations. Thus they cannot be counted; and Abram's seed was to be countless, because of the vastness of its number.

6.pericope_label: And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness

schools.summary: Gill takes the object of the believing as widely as the promise allows, following the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, which read it as believing in the Word of the Lord: in the essential Word of the Lord, in Christ the Lord his righteousness. Abram believed the promise of God that he should have a seed, and a very numerous one; he believed that the Messiah would spring from his seed; he believed in him as his Saviour and Redeemer; he believed in him for righteousness, and he believed in his righteousness as justifying him before God. Calvin says that none of us would be able to conceive the rich and hidden doctrine which this passage contains, unless Paul had borne his torch before us; and it seems like a prodigy that, when the Spirit of God has kindled so great a light, the greater part of interpreters should wander with closed eyes as in the darkness of night. In all ages, he says, Satan has laboured at nothing more assiduously than to extinguish or to smother the gratuitous justification of faith which is here expressly asserted. Two things are commended in the words: the faith of Abram, because by it he embraced the promise of God; and then that hence Abram obtained righteousness in the sight of God, and that by imputation. The verb Moses uses is to be understood as relating to the judgment of God, and its force appears best by comparison with its opposites — when expiation has been made, iniquity shall not be imputed to a man; blood shall be imputed unto that man; let not the king impute iniquity unto me. Just as those to whom iniquity is imputed are guilty before God, so those to whom he imputes righteousness are approved by him as just persons. Therefore they trifle who apply the term to Abram's character as an honest man, as if it meant that he was personally held to be just; and they no less corrupt the text who say that Abram is here ascribing to God the glory of righteousness. To the objection that it seems absurd for Abram to be justified by believing that his seed would be as numerous as the stars, since this could be nothing but a particular faith, Calvin answers that the faith of which Moses speaks is not to be restricted to a single clause of the promise but embraces the whole, and that Abram did not form his estimate of the promised seed from this oracle alone but from others where a special benediction is added. We do not say that Abram was justified because he laid hold on a single word respecting the offspring to be brought forth, but because he embraced God as his Father; and faith does not justify us for any other reason than that it reconciles us unto God, not by its own merit, but because we receive the grace offered in the promises. Calvin then presses the date. Abram was justified by faith many years after he had been called by God, after he had left his country a voluntary exile, after he had rendered himself a remarkable example of patience and continence, and after he had aspired, by exercising himself in the service of God, to a life almost angelical; and it therefore follows that even to the end of life we are led towards the eternal kingdom of God by the righteousness of faith. Many are grossly deceived here, granting that the righteousness freely bestowed upon sinners is received by faith alone, but restricting this to a moment of time, so that he who at the first obtained justification by faith may afterwards be justified by good works, faith being nothing but the beginning of righteousness. If the angelical uprightness of Abram, faithfully cultivated through so many years in one uniform course, did not prevent him from fleeing to faith for the sake of obtaining righteousness, where upon earth shall such perfection be found as may stand in God's sight? Holy men are only justified by faith as long as they live in the world; and what is here related concerning one man is applicable to all the sons of God, since he was not without reason called the father of the faithful, and there is but one method of obtaining salvation.

Clarke conceives this to be one of the most important passages in the whole Old Testament, since it properly contains and specifies that doctrine of justification by faith which engrosses so considerable a share of the epistles of Paul, and at the foundation of which is the atonement made by the Son of God. He glosses the two Hebrew verbs in turn — Abram put faith in Jehovah, and God counted it, the faith he put in Jehovah, to him for righteousness or justification — and draws the conclusion from the absence of any deed: though there was no act in the case but that of the mind and heart, no work of any kind, hence comes the doctrine of justification by faith without any merit of works, for in this case there could be none, no works of Abram which could merit the salvation of the whole human race. It was the promise of God which he credited, and in the blessedness of which he became a partaker through faith. Wesley keeps rather to the temper of the believing. Abram believed the truth of that promise which God had now made him, resting upon the power and faithfulness of him that made it, and the apostle magnifies this faith and makes it a standing example — he was not weak in faith, he staggered not at the promise, he was strong in faith, he was fully persuaded. Upon the score of this he was accepted of God, and by faith obtained witness that he was righteous; and this is urged in the New Testament to prove that we are justified by faith without the works of the law, since Abram was so justified while he was yet uncircumcised. If Abram, who was so rich in good works, was not justified by them but by his faith, much less can we. Wesley adds that this faith had newly struggled with unbelief in the complaint just made, and, coming off conqueror, was thus crowned and thus honoured.

Ellicott calls the verse the germ of the doctrine of free justification, and rests the weight of the argument on the place the narrator gave it. Abram was both a holy man and one who proved his faith by his works; but nevertheless the inspired narrator inserts this reflection, not after the history of the offering of Isaac, where the works would have been in view, but in the account of this vision, where all that Abram did was to believe, and for that belief's sake was accounted righteous before God. For the definite conclusions deduced from the verse Ellicott refers the reader to the fourth chapter of Romans, noting that the quotation there is from the Septuagint and gives the general sense, while the correct rendering of the Hebrew is that given in our version.

7.pericope_label: I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it. And he said, Whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?

schools.summary: Henry observes first that Abram made no complaint in this matter, as he had done for the want of a child: those who are sure of an interest in the promised seed will see no reason to doubt of a title to the promised land, for if Christ is ours, heaven is ours; and when he believed the former promise, then God explained and ratified this one to him, since to him that has, more shall be given. Three things God reminds him of for his encouragement. What God is in himself: I am Jehovah, and therefore I may give it thee, being sovereign Lord of all and having a right to dispose of the whole earth; I can give it thee, whatever opposition may be made, even by the sons of Anak, for God never promises more than he is able to perform, as men often do; and I will make good my promise, for Jehovah is not a man that he should lie. What he had done for Abram: he had brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, out of the fire of the Chaldees, so some read it, either from their idolatries, since the Chaldeans worshipped the fire, or from their persecutions. It was a special mercy, for God called him alone and left thousands to perish there; a spiritual mercy, a deliverance from sin and its fatal consequences; a fresh mercy, lately bestowed and therefore the more affecting; and a foundation mercy, the beginning of mercy and therefore a pledge and earnest of further mercy. And what he intended yet to do: I brought thee hither on purpose to give thee this land to inherit it, not only to possess it but to possess it as an inheritance, which is the sweetest and surest title; for the providence of God has secret but gracious designs in all its dispensations toward good people, and the great thing God designs in all his dealings with them is to bring them safely to heaven. On the request that follows, Henry denies that it proceeded from distrust of God's power or promise, as that of Zacharias did. Abram desired it for the strengthening of his own faith — he believed, but here he prays, Lord, help me against my unbelief, desiring a sign to be treasured up against an hour of temptation, not knowing how his faith might by some event be shocked and tried; and for the ratifying of the promise to his posterity, that they also might be brought to believe it, since those who are satisfied themselves should desire that others also may be satisfied of the truth of God's promises. Canaan was a type of heaven, and it is a very desirable thing to know that we shall inherit the heavenly Canaan.

Gill defends the asking of a sign at length. Abram put the question not as questioning or doubting whether he should inherit the land, but for the further confirmation of his own faith in the promise, and for the sake of his posterity, that they might more easily and strongly believe that they should inherit the land given and promised to them; nor is it culpable to ask a sign of God with such a view, since good men have done it — Gideon and Hezekiah — without being blamed for it, and Ahaz is blamed for not asking one. Calvin feels the objection more sharply and answers it at greater length. It may appear absurd, first, that Abram, who before had placed confidence in the simple word of God without moving any question concerning the promises, should now dispute whether what he hears from the mouth of God be true; and secondly, that he ascribes but little honour to God by requiring some additional pledge. Further, whence arises the knowledge which belongs to faith, but from the word? The answer is that the Lord sometimes concedes to his children that they may freely express any objection which comes into their mind, for he does not act so strictly with them as not to suffer himself to be questioned. Yea, the more certainly Abram was persuaded that God was true, and the more he was attached to his word, so much the more familiarly did he disburden his cares into God's bosom. To this may be added that the protracted delay was no small obstacle to his faith: after God had held him in suspense through a great part of his life, now when he was worn down with age and had nothing before his eyes but death and the grave, God anew declares that he shall be lord of the land. He does not reject as incredible what might have appeared so, but brings before God the anxiety by which he is inwardly oppressed; and therefore his questioning with God is rather a proof of faith than a sign of incredulity. The wicked, because their minds are entangled with various conflicting thoughts, do not in any way receive the promises; but the pious, who feel the impediments in their flesh, endeavour to remove them, lest they should obstruct the way to God's word. It is nevertheless to be observed, Calvin adds, that there were some special impulses in the saints of old which it would not now be lawful to draw into a precedent; though Hezekiah and Gideon required certain miracles, this is no reason why the same should be attempted in the present day. On the preceding verse he notes that the Lord confirms Abram in the course of his vocation and recalls to his memory the original benefit of his deliverance, connecting the promise he is about to give with the prior redemption: I do not now first begin to promise thee this land, for it was on this account that I brought thee out of thy own country.

Wesley follows Henry on the deliverance from Ur, repeating the Jewish tradition that Abram was cast into a fiery furnace for refusing to worship idols and was miraculously delivered, though judging it rather to be a place of that name; thence God brought him by an effectual call, brought him by a gracious violence, snatched him as a brand out of the burning. He notes how God speaks of it as a thing he glories in, as an act both of power and grace; and that the land was to be possessed not merely as a holding but as an inheritance, which is the surest title. The providence of God, he adds, has secret but gracious designs in all its various dispensations, and we cannot conceive the projects of providence till the event shows what it was driving at. On the request for a sign Wesley denies that it proceeded from distrust of God's power or promise: Abram desired it for the strengthening of his own faith — he believed, but here he prays, Lord, help me against my unbelief; he desired a sign to be treasured up against an hour of temptation; and he desired it for the ratifying of the promise to his posterity, that they also might believe it. Clarke contributes chiefly a note on the divine title Abram uses in the request, which the Jews always substitute for the ineffable name, counting it impious to pronounce that. The word signifies my director, basis, supporter, prop or stay, and Clarke thinks scarcely a more appropriate name can be given to that God who is the framer and director of every righteous word and action, the basis on which every rational hope rests, the supporter of the souls and bodies of men as well as of the universe in general, the prop and stay of the weak and fainting, and the buttress that shores up the building which otherwise must necessarily fall.

Ellicott explains the request from what had gone before. Jehovah had required Abram to leave his home in Ur of the Chaldees on a general promise of future endowment with the land of Canaan; Abram now asks his question, not from want of faith, but from a desire for a more direct confirmation of the promise and a fuller knowledge of the details. What Abram therefore receives is an exact and circumstantial prophecy, made in the form of a solemn covenant. He notes also that the title used is Lord Jehovah, as at the earlier complaint. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same judgment in a sentence: Abram's question, whereby shall I know that I shall take possession of the land, was not an expression of doubt, but of desire for the confirmation or sealing of a promise which transcended human thought.

9.pericope_label: Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat, and a ram, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon; he divided them in the midst, and drove away the fowls

schools.summary: Clarke works through the five creatures name by name, noting the Hebrew of each and the sense of the adjective rendered three years old, and then draws a conclusion from the list as a whole: it is worthy of remark that every animal allowed or commanded to be sacrificed under the Mosaic law is to be found here. Is this not a proof, he asks, that God was now giving to Abram an epitome of that law and its sacrifices which he intended more fully to reveal to Moses, the essence of which consisted in its sacrifices, and these typified the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world? He then passes on the reading of Jarchi: the idolatrous nations are compared in the Scriptures to bulls, rams and goats, while the Israelites are compared to doves; the division of the carcasses denotes the division and extermination of the idolatrous nations, but the birds not being divided shows that the Israelites are to abide for ever. On the dividing itself Clarke sets out the ancient rite at length. A covenant supposes at least two parties, since it is impossible that one can be made between an individual and himself, and often there was a third party to mediate and to witness it. He lists four things a covenant supposes: that the parties had been hitherto unknown to each other; that they had been in a state of enmity and were brought to friendship; that being known to each other they now agree to unite their counsels and strength for a common purpose; or that they agree to succour a third party in oppression and distress. For whatever purpose it was made, it was ever ratified by a sacrifice offered to God, and the passing between the divided parts appears to have signified that each agreed, if he broke his engagements, to submit to the punishment of being cut asunder — a mode of punishment Clarke documents from Matthew and Luke, from Herodotus, who reports both the vision of Sabacus and the fate of the son of Pythius, and from Daniel. He preserves also the form of imprecation Livy records from the league between the Romans and the Albans, where the priest, before slaying the victim, called on Jupiter so to smite the Roman people if they should first transgress. Of the one exception he says only that according to the later law fowls were not to be divided asunder, but only cloven. Wesley, following Henry, observes that perhaps Abram expected some extraordinary sign from heaven, and that God gives him a sign upon a sacrifice: those who would receive the assurances of God's favour must attend instituted ordinances and expect to meet with God in them. Each beast was to be three years old because then they were at their full growth and strength, and God must be served with the best we have. We do not read that God gave particular directions how to manage them, knowing that Abram was well versed in the custom of sacrifices; and Abram took as God appointed him, though as yet he knew not how these things should become a sign to him. Having prepared according to the appointment, he set himself to expect what sign God would give him by these.

Gill reads the whole preparation as emblematic: this, with what follows, is the sign by which Abram might know that his seed should inherit the land of Canaan, the whole being an emblem of the state and condition of his posterity until they should enter into it. He notes that the creatures were used in sacrifice before the ceremonial law was given as well as under it, and that the distinction of creatures for sacrifice, though not for food, was known as early as the ark; Onkelos renders the command "offer before me," and the Targum of Jonathan, "take unto me oblations, and offer before me." He marks one difference to be observed: the Levitical law required creatures of a year old only to be offered, whereas these were three years old, because they are then at their full growth and in their greatest perfection, and such were used among the heathen also. Of the birds of prey Gill says they are to be understood of eagles, vultures, kites and the like, and are an emblem chiefly of the Egyptians and the other enemies of Israel who came upon them to devour them; the Targum of Jonathan reads that the idolatrous nations descended, who were like to an unclean fowl, to spoil the goods of the Israelites, and the Jerusalem Targum, that this unclean fowl are the idolatrous kingdoms of the earth. Calvin refuses to allegorise every detail: certain interpreters weary themselves in the fabrication of subtleties, but it is our business to cultivate sobriety, and he confesses he does not know why three kinds of animals were commanded besides the birds, unless it were that by the variety itself it was declared that all the posterity of Abram, of whatever rank, should be offered up, so that the whole people and each individual should constitute one sacrifice. The sum of the whole, in his judgment, is that God, in commanding the animals to be killed, shows what will be the future condition of the Church. Abram wished to be assured of the promised inheritance, and is now taught that it would take its commencement from death: he and his children must die before they should enjoy the dominion over the land. In commanding the slaughtered animals to be cut in parts it is probable that God followed the ancient rite in forming covenants, where the allies or the soldiers passed between the severed parts, that, being enclosed together within the sacrifice, they might be the more sacredly united in one body — a practice to which Jeremiah bears witness among the Jews. Yet Calvin finds a special reason here besides: the Lord would admonish the race of Abram not only that it should be like a dead carcass, but even like one torn and dissected, since the servitude with which they were oppressed was more intolerable than simple death. Because the sacrifice is offered to God, death itself is immediately turned into new life; and this is why Abram, placing the parts opposite to each other, fits them one to the other, because they were again to be gathered together from their dispersion. Of the birds of prey he adds that although the sacrifice was dedicated to God it was not free from their attack and violence; so neither are the faithful, after they are received into the protection of God, so covered with his hand as not to be assailed on every side, since Satan and the world cease not to trouble them. Therefore, in order that the sacrifice we have once offered may remain pure and uninjured, contrary assaults must be repulsed, with whatever inconvenience and toil.

Ellicott renders the clause more exactly than our version — the birds of prey came down upon the carcases, and Abram scared them away — and explains why the guarding was needed. Had there been a sacrifice properly so called, the fire would have kept the vultures from approaching; but the bodies lay exposed, and Abram therefore kept guard over them, lest the purpose of the ceremonial should be frustrated by any want of respect shown to the outward symbols.

12.pericope_label: When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and an horror of great darkness; know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs

schools.summary: Henry sets the hour of the discovery against the whole day of waiting. Early in the morning, before day, while the stars were yet to be seen, God had given Abram his orders concerning the sacrifices, and we may suppose it was at least his morning's work to prepare them and set them in order; when he had done this, he abode by them, praying and waiting till towards evening, about the time of the evening oblation. God often keeps his people long in expectation of the comforts he designs them, for the confirmation of their faith; but though the answers of prayer and the performance of promises come slowly, yet they come surely, and at evening time it shall be light. Of the preparatives Henry notes two. A deep sleep fell upon Abram, not a common sleep through weariness or carelessness, but a divine ecstasy, like that which the Lord caused to fall upon Adam, so that, being wholly taken off from the view of things sensible, he might be wholly taken up with the contemplation of things spiritual — the doors of the body locked up, that the soul might be private and retired, and might act the more freely and like itself. And with this sleep a horror of great darkness fell upon him: how sudden a change, when just before we had him solacing himself in the comforts of God's covenant and in communion with him. The children of light do not always walk in the light, but sometimes clouds and darkness are round about them. Henry gives the darkness three designs: to strike an awe upon the spirit of Abram and possess him with a holy reverence, that the familiarity to which God was pleased to admit him might not breed contempt, for holy fear prepares the soul for holy joy, and God wounds first and then heals, humbles first and then lifts up; to be a specimen of the methods of God's dealings with his seed, who must first be in the horror and darkness of Egyptian slavery and then enter with joy into the good land, so that Abram must have the foretaste of their sufferings before the foresight of their happiness; and to indicate the nature of that covenant of peculiarity God was now about to make, since the Old Testament dispensation founded upon it was one of darkness and obscurity, and of dread and horror. Of the prediction itself he says that God sends the worst first — we must first suffer and then reign — and lets us know the worst before it comes, that when it comes it may not surprise us. Abram must not flatter himself with the hopes of nothing but honour and prosperity in his family; he must know of a surety that the promised seed should be a persecuted seed. They shall be strangers, first in Canaan and afterwards in Egypt, for before they were lords of their own land they were strangers in a strange land, as the heirs of heaven are first strangers on earth. They shall be servants, and what was the doom of the Canaanites proves the distress of Abram's seed, with this difference, that the Canaanites serve under a curse and the Hebrews under a blessing. And they shall be sufferers, since those whom they serve shall afflict them, and those that are blessed and beloved of God are often sorely afflicted by wicked men, and God foresees it and takes cognizance of it. The term was long, but it was a limited term.

Gill lingers on the hour, the sun just setting, descending below the hemisphere, or about to enter into his chamber, whence he went forth in the morning as a strong man to run his race; and at the following verse he notes only that God said this to Abram while he was in a deep sleep, in a vision of prophecy. Calvin observes that the vision is now mingled with a dream, the Lord joining together the two kinds of communication which he elsewhere names when he says that he speaks to his prophets in a vision or a dream. Mention has already been made of a vision, and Moses now relates that a dream was superadded; a horrible darkness intervened, that Abram might know the dream was not a common one, but that the whole was divinely conducted. Calvin adds a rule he often repeats, that God was not wont to dazzle the eyes of his people with bare and empty spectres, but that in visions the principal parts always belonged to the word: here not a mute apparition is presented to the eyes of Abram, but he is taught by an oracle annexed what the external and visible symbol meant. It is to be observed, he says, that before one son is given to Abram, he hears that his seed shall be for a long time in captivity and slavery; for thus does the Lord deal with his own people, always making a beginning from death, so that by quickening the dead he may the more abundantly manifest his power. This was needful in part on Abram's own account, but the Lord chiefly had regard to his posterity, lest they should faint in their sufferings, of which he had nevertheless promised a joyful and happy issue, especially since their long continuance would produce great weariness. Three things are brought before them step by step: that the sons of Abram must wander before they attain the promised inheritance; that they should be slaves; and that they were to be inhumanly and tyrannically treated. Wherefore the faith of Abram was admirable and singular, seeing that he acquiesced in an oracle so sorrowful, and felt assured that God would be his Deliverer after his miseries had proceeded to their greatest height. On the reckoning of the years Calvin rejects the computation which begins from the departure out of Charran, and holds it more probable that the intermediate time only is denoted, as if God had said, It behoves thy posterity to wait patiently, because I have not decreed to grant what I now promise until that term is out. So Moses elsewhere says that the children of Israel dwelt in Egypt a longer period than the sojourn itself can have taken, and Paul removes all doubt by reckoning the years from the gratuitous covenant of life to the promulgation of the Law. In short, God does not indicate how long the servitude of the people should be from its commencement to its close, but how long he intended to suspend or to defer his promise; and it is neither new nor infrequent, where years are not accurately computed, to mention only the larger sums.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the point at which the vision changes character: here it passes into a prophetic sleep produced by God, the deep sleep being the same word used of the sleep that fell on Adam. In that sleep there fell upon Abram dread and darkness, and the interchange of the perfect and the participle in the Hebrew shows the one falling upon the other. The reference to the time, they say, is intended to show the supernatural character of the darkness and the sleep, and the distinction between the vision and a dream; but it also possesses a symbolical meaning, since the setting of the sun prefigured to Abram the departure of the sun of grace which shone upon Israel, and the commencement of a dark and dreadful period of suffering for his posterity, the very anticipation of which involved Abram in darkness. Ellicott reconstructs the sequence of the day. The time described was the evening following the night on which Abram had received the assurance that his seed should be countless as the stars; he had then, in his trance, also asked for security that Canaan should be the heritage of his posterity, and in answer had received the command to arrange, upon a large scale, the ceremonial of a solemn treaty-making. The morning had been spent in performing the command, and afterwards he had watched, probably for several hours, by the side of the divided bodies, uncertain what would happen, but occupied in driving away the vultures which gathered from all quarters round the abundant feast. At sunset the revelation came to him, not in a waking trance as on the previous night, but in a deep sleep, and with those accompaniments of terror so powerfully described in the book of Job, which the creature cannot but feel when brought near to the manifest presence of the Creator. Of the terror itself Ellicott would render the Hebrew, lo, a terror, even great darkness, falling upon him, and holds that it was not mental so much as bodily, caused by a deep gloom settling round him, such as would be the effect of an eclipse of the setting sun, and shutting all mortal things away from his view.

Clarke identifies the deep sleep by its Hebrew name as the same word used to express the sleep into which Adam was cast previous to the formation of Eve, and says of the horror of great darkness that God designed it to be expressive of the affliction and misery into which the posterity of Abram should be brought during the years of their bondage in Egypt, as the next verse particularly states. On the term of years he passes on the reckoning of Ainsworth, which begins the persecution when the son of Hagar mocked and persecuted Isaac, thirty years after the promise, and counts from the promise to the law and from the promise to the coming out of Egypt. Wesley, following Henry, marks the hour as about the time of the evening oblation, and notes that early in the morning, while the stars were yet to be seen, God had given Abram his orders concerning the sacrifices, so that it was at least his morning's work to prepare them and set them in order, after which he abode by them praying and waiting till towards evening. The sleep that then fell upon him was not a common sleep through weariness or carelessness, but a divine ecstasy, that, being wholly taken off from things sensible, he might be wholly taken up with the contemplation of things spiritual, the doors of the body locked up that the soul might be private and retired and might act the more freely. The horror of great darkness was designed to strike an awe upon his spirit and to possess him with a holy reverence, for holy fear prepares the soul for holy joy, and God humbles first and then lifts up. Of the prediction Wesley keeps Henry's three heads, that they shall be strangers, first in Canaan and afterwards in Egypt, for before they were lords of their own land they were strangers in a strange land; that they shall serve, as they did the Egyptians, though with this difference, that the Canaanites serve under a curse and the Hebrews under a blessing; and that they shall be afflicted, since those that are blessed and beloved of God are often afflicted by wicked men. This persecution began with mocking and came at last to murder, the basest of murders, that of their new-born children.

14.pericope_label: That nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge; and thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age

schools.summary: Gill fastens on the precision of the word: it is not said the land in which they were strangers, though God did judge and punish the inhabitants of the land of Canaan and drove them out to make way for Israel, but the nation they should serve, meaning the Egyptians, to whom they became servants and were very hardly and severely used by them. Those the Lord threatens to enter into judgment with and take vengeance upon, as he did by inflicting the ten plagues upon them, which brought them at last to be willing to let Israel go. Of the promise to Abram himself Gill says that to go to the fathers is to die, which is going the way of all flesh, to a man's long home, out of this world to another, to the world of spirits, to those that are gone before — no inconsiderable proof, he adds, of the immortality of the soul. Jarchi infers from the phrase that Terah, Abram's father, was a penitent and died a good man; but Gill observes that the phrase of going to the fathers is used both of good and of bad men. What is peculiar to Abram is that he should go in peace, being freed from all the fatigues of his journeying from place to place in his state of pilgrimage, and not living to see the afflictions of his posterity or to have any share in them, and dying in spiritual peace and tranquillity of mind, knowing in whom he had believed and where his salvation was safe and secure. Calvin takes the judgment of the oppressor as a consolation subjoined to the threat, of which the first thing is that God testifies he will be the vindicator of his people; whence it follows that he will take upon himself the care of the salvation of those whom he has embraced, and will not suffer them to be harassed by the ungodly with impunity. Although he here expressly announces vengeance on the Egyptians, all the enemies of the Church are exposed to the same judgment, even as Moses in his song extends to all ages and nations the threat that the Lord will exact punishment for unjust persecutions. Therefore, whenever we happen to be treated with inhumanity by tyrants, which is very usual with the Church, let this be our consolation: that after our faith shall be sufficiently proved by bearing the cross, God, at whose pleasure we are thus humbled, will himself be the Judge, and will repay to our enemies the due reward of the cruelty which they now exercise. Although they now exult with intoxicated joy, it will at length appear by the event itself that our miseries are happy ones and their triumphs wretched, because God, who cares for us, is their adversary; but we must remember to give place unto the wrath of God, as Paul exhorts, that we may not be hurried headlong to seek revenge, and place must be given to hope also, that it may sustain us when oppressed and groaning under the burden of evils. To judge the nation, he explains, means the same as to summon it to judgment, in order that God, when he has long reposed in silence, may openly manifest himself as the Judge. Turning to Abram alone, Calvin says the remedy proposed for alleviating his sorrow was that he should die in peace, after he had attained the utmost limit of old age. The explanation given by some, that he should die a natural death exempt from violence, or an easy death in which his vital spirits should spontaneously fail without any sense of pain, is in his opinion frigid; Moses wishes to express that Abram should have not only a long but a placid old age, with a corresponding joyful and peaceful death. Although through his whole life he was to be deprived of the possession of the land, yet he should not be wanting in the essential materials of quiet and joy, so that, having happily finished his life, he should cheerfully depart to his fathers. And certainly death makes the great distinction between the reprobate and the sons of God, whose condition in the present life is commonly one and the same, except that the sons of God have by far the worst of it; wherefore peace in death ought justly to be regarded as a singular benefit. Even profane writers, feeling their way in the dark, have perceived this, and Calvin cites the song of Pindar quoted by Plato, that they who live justly and holily are attended by a sweet hope, cherishing their hearts and nourishing their old age. Since men have not such a desirable close of life in their own power, the Lord, in promising a placid and quiet death to his servant, teaches us that it is his own gift; and we see that even kings and others who deem themselves happy in this world are yet agitated in death, while Abram willingly and joyfully went forward to his, seeing that he had in Isaac a certain pledge of the divine benediction, and knew that a better life was laid up for him in heaven.

Clarke measures the promise by its fulfilment: how remarkably was this fulfilled, he exclaims, in the redemption of Israel from its bondage, in the plagues and destruction of the Egyptians, and in the immense wealth which the Israelites brought out of Egypt — not a more circumstantial or literally fulfilled promise is to be found in the sacred writings. On the promise made to Abram himself he finds a doctrine implied: the verse strongly implies the immortality of the soul and a state of separate existence, for Abram was gathered to his fathers, introduced into the place where separate spirits are kept, waiting for the general resurrection. Two things seem to Clarke to be distinctly marked here — that the soul of Abram should be introduced among the assembly of the first-born, in the words thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; and that his body should be buried after a long life of a hundred and seventy-five years. The body was buried; the soul went to the spiritual world, to dwell among the fathers, the patriarchs who had lived and died in the Lord. Wesley, following Henry, reads the judgment of the Egyptians as pointing at the plagues, by which God not only constrained them to release Israel but punished them for all the hardships they had put upon them; the punishing of persecutors is the judging of them, and it is a righteous thing with God, and a particular act of justice, to recompense tribulation to those that trouble his people. Afterwards they should come out with great substance, either after the appointed term of affliction or after the Egyptians are judged and plagued. Of the death promised to Abram, Wesley says that at death we go to our fathers, to all our fathers that are gone before us to the state of the dead, and to our godly fathers that are gone before us to the state of the blessed; the former helps to take off the terror of death, the latter puts comfort into it. Perhaps mention is made of his burial here, where the land of Canaan is promised him, because a burying-place was the first possession he had in it. Old age is a blessing if it be a good old age: theirs may be called a good old age that are old and healthful, not loaded with such distempers as make them weary of life; that are old and holy, whose hoary head is found in the way of righteousness; old and useful, old and exemplary for godliness.

Ellicott explains why the oppressing country is left unnamed. Had it been expressly revealed that the land which would afflict them was Egypt, the patriarchs might have been unwilling to go thither; but the reference to the plagues in the denunciation of judgment, and to the spoiling of the Egyptians in the promise that they should come out with great substance, gave detail sufficient for future guidance, and for their assurance in time to come that the promise had been fulfilled. Of the words spoken to Abram himself he observes that Abram's ancestors had died in Babylonia, so that the phrase, used here for the first time, evidently involves the thought of the immortality of the soul: the body may be buried far away, but the soul joins the company of its forefathers in some separate abode, not to be absorbed, but still to enjoy a personal existence. A similar, though more exact, distinction between the body and the spirit is drawn at the close of Ecclesiastes.

16.pericope_label: But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full

schools.summary: Gill takes the fourth generation of those who went down into Egypt, since Moses and Aaron were the fourth from Levi, or Eleazar from Kohath, and Caleb from Judah; or rather, he suggests, it was the fourth age or century reckoned from the birth of Isaac, men living at that time about a hundred years apiece. He notes that Grotius interpreted the phrase instead of the fourth generation of the Amorites, because of the clause which follows. Calvin meets head-on the objection that the reason here given is absurd, as seeming to imply that the sons of Abram could not otherwise be saved than by the destruction of others. We must, he answers, with modesty and humility yield to the secret counsel of God. Since God had given that land to the Amorites, to be inhabited by them in perpetuity, he intimates that he will not without just cause transfer the possession of it to others; as if he would say, I grant the dominion of this land to thy seed without injury to any one, for the land at present is occupied by its lawful possessors, to whom I delivered it, and until they shall have deserved by their sins to be rightfully expelled, the dominion of it will not come to thy posterity. Thus God teaches him that the land must be evacuated in order that it may lie open to new inhabitants. This passage is remarkable, Calvin says, as showing that the abodes of men are so distributed in the world that the Lord will preserve quiet people, each in their several stations, till they cast themselves out by their own wickedness; for by polluting the place of their habitation they in a certain sense tear away the boundaries fixed by the hand of God, which would otherwise have remained immovable. Moreover, the Lord here commends his own longsuffering: even then the Amorites had become unworthy to occupy the land, yet the Lord not only bore with them for a short time but granted them centuries for repentance; and hence it appears that he does not without reason so frequently declare how slow he is to anger. But the more graciously he waits for men, if at length, instead of repenting, they remain obstinate, the more severely does he avenge such great ingratitude; therefore Paul says that they who indulge themselves in sin while the goodness and clemency of God invite them to repentance heap up for themselves a treasure of wrath, and thus they reap no advantage from delay, seeing that the severity of the punishment is doubled — just as it happened to the Amorites, whom at length the Lord commanded to be so entirely cut off that not even infants were spared. Therefore, when we hear that God out of heaven is silently waiting until iniquities shall fill up their measure, let us know that this is no time for torpor, but rather let every one of us stir himself up, that we may be beforehand with the celestial judgment. It was formerly said by a heathen that the anger of God proceeds with a slow step to avenge itself, but that it compensates for its tardiness by the severity of its punishment; hence there is no reason why reprobates should flatter themselves when he seems to let them pass unobserved, since he does not so repose in heaven as to cease to be the Judge of the world. We infer, however, from the words of Moses, that though space for repentance is given to the reprobate, they are still devoted to destruction.

Ellicott takes the generations here to be identical with the centuries named earlier in the chapter, and finds in the equation an undesigned testimony to the long duration of human life in that age: Abram was a hundred years old when Isaac was born, Isaac sixty at the birth of his children, and Jacob sixty-four at his marriage. He adds that the Hebrew word had probably come down from a remote antiquity and, like the Latin seculum, signified a century. Of the Amorites he says that, as the chief and leading tribe, they are used here for all the Canaanite nations, and he makes the clause govern the whole conquest: we learn from this declaration that the Canaanites were not extirpated by any wilful decree to make room for Israel, but as an act of justice, like that which, because of their moral depravity, overwhelmed the men of the earlier world with a flood. So, subsequently, Israel and Judah had each to bear a punishment in accordance with their sinfulness; and so, throughout the history of the world, whenever nations settle down in vice and corruption, the decay of their institutions follows upon that of their morals, and they either waste away or give place to some more manly race of conquerors. The conquest of Canaan by Israel was parallel to that of the enervated Roman empire of the West by the Germans; only here we see the preparation for it, and God's purpose explained, and we also see that if the Amorites had not made the scale of justice weigh down heavily, they would not have been deprived of their country.

Clarke observes that in former times most peoples counted by generations, and that to each of these was assigned a term of years which varied widely from nation to nation and age to age — twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-three, or as much as a hundred and ten. It is probable, he thinks, that the fourth generation here means the same span as the figure given in the preceding sentence. Some think it refers to the time when Eleazar, the son of Aaron, came out of Egypt and divided the land of Canaan to Israel; others think the fourth generation of the Amorites is intended, because it is immediately added that their iniquity is not yet full, and in the fourth generation they should be expelled and the descendants of Abram established in their place. From these words, Clarke concludes, we learn that there is a certain pitch of iniquity to which nations may arrive before they are destroyed, and beyond which divine justice does not permit them to pass. Wesley, following Henry, gives the reason why they must not have the land of promise in possession until then: it is because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full, the righteous God having determined that they should not be cut off till they were arrived at such a pitch of wickedness; and therefore, till it come to that, the seed of Abram must be kept out of possession.

17.pericope_label: A smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed between those pieces; in the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land

schools.summary: Henry treats the appearance as the covenant ratified: the sign Abram had desired was given at length, when the sun had gone down so that it was dark, for that was a dark dispensation. The smoking furnace signified the affliction of his seed in Egypt, where they were in the iron furnace, the furnace of affliction, labouring in the very fire; they were there in the smoke, their eyes darkened that they could not see to the end of their troubles, and themselves at a loss to conceive what God would do with them, clouds and darkness being round about them. The burning lamp denotes comfort in that affliction, and God showed it to Abram at the same time that he showed him the furnace. Light denotes deliverance out of the furnace, their salvation being as a lamp that burneth, and when God came down to deliver them he appeared in a bush that burned and was not consumed. The lamp denotes direction in the smoke, since God's word was their lamp, a light shining in a dark place, and perhaps this burning lamp prefigured the pillar of cloud and fire which led them out of Egypt. And the burning lamp denotes the destruction of their enemies who kept them so long in the furnace, for the same cloud that enlightened the Israelites troubled and burned the Egyptians. The passing of these between the pieces was the confirming of the covenant God now made with him, that he might have strong consolation, being fully persuaded that what God promised he would certainly perform; and it is probable that the furnace and lamp burnt and consumed the pieces, so completing the sacrifice and testifying God's acceptance of it, as fire did for Gideon, for Manoah, and for Solomon. Thus it intimates that God's covenants with man are made by sacrifice, by Christ the great sacrifice — no agreement without atonement; and that God's acceptance of our spiritual sacrifices is a token for good and an earnest of further favours, by which we may know that he accepts them, if he kindle in our souls a holy fire of pious and devout affections. Of the grant Henry notes the change of tense: God had said before, to thy seed will I give this land, but here he says, I have given it, that is, the promise of it, the charter sealed and delivered and not to be disannulled, and the possession as sure in due time as if it were now actually delivered — for God's promises are God's gifts, and what God has promised is as sure as if it were already done. Then follows a recital of the particulars granted, such as is usual in the grants of lands: the boundaries are specified, and, for the greater certainty, the tenure and occupation in which the lands then were, ten nations being named that must be cast out to make room for the seed of Abram. Henry gives three reasons why the grant is stated so widely. In David's time and Solomon's their jurisdiction extended to the utmost of these limits; it was their own fault that they were not sooner and longer in possession of all these territories, since they forfeited their right by their sins and by their own sloth and cowardice kept themselves out; and the land is described in its utmost extent because it was to be a type of the heavenly inheritance, where there is room enough, since in our Father's house are many mansions. The present occupants are named so that their number and strength and long prescription should be no hindrance to the accomplishment of the promise in its season, and to magnify God's love to Abram and his seed in giving to that one nation the possessions of many nations.

Clarke thinks the smoking furnace might be designed as an emblem of the sore afflictions of the Israelites in Egypt, but is decided about the other symbol: the burning lamp was certainly the symbol of the divine presence, which, passing between the pieces, ratified the covenant with Abram, as the following verse immediately states. On the making of the covenant he explains the Hebrew idiom, which signifies to cut a covenant, or rather the covenant sacrifice; for as no covenant was made without one, and the creature was cut in two that the contracting parties might pass between the pieces, hence cutting the covenant signified making the covenant. The same form of speech obtained among the Romans, who, because in making their covenants they always slew an animal and divided the parts, used the phrases to smite a covenant and to cleave a covenant to signify simply entering into one. Of the southern boundary Clarke dissents from the common view: the river of Egypt is not the Nile, he holds, but the river called Sichor, which was before or on the border of Egypt, near to the isthmus of Suez, though some think that a branch of the Nile is meant. This promise, he adds, was fully accomplished in the days of David and Solomon. Wesley, following Henry, reads the smoking furnace of the affliction of the seed in Egypt, where they were in the furnace of affliction and labouring in the very fire, in the smoke, their eyes darkened that they could not see to the end of their troubles; and the burning lamp as comfort in that affliction, a lamp for direction in the smoke, God's word being their lamp shining in a dark place, and perhaps prefiguring the pillar of cloud and fire that led them out of Egypt. The passing of these between the pieces confirmed the covenant, and it is probable they burnt and consumed the pieces, completing the sacrifice and testifying God's acceptance of it, as with Gideon and Manoah and Solomon; so it intimates that God's covenants with man are made by sacrifice, by Christ the great sacrifice. Wesley adds Henry's note on the grant, that in the days of David and Solomon their jurisdiction reached the utmost of these limits, that it was their own fault they were not sooner and longer in possession of all these territories, since they forfeited their right by their sins and by sloth and cowardice kept themselves out, and that the present occupants are named to magnify God's love in giving to that one nation the possession of many nations.

Gill notes only the hour, that the sun was going down when the deep sleep fell upon Abram and was now quite set, and that the covenant was confirmed by God's passing between the pieces and accepting the sacrifice. Calvin sees in the burning lamp a second vision added to confirm Abram's faith in the oracle. At first he was horror-struck with the thick darkness; now, in the midst of a smoking furnace, he sees a burning lamp. Many suppose that a sacrifice was consumed with this fire, but Calvin rather interprets it as a symbol of future deliverance, which would well agree with the fact itself; for there are two things contrary to each other in appearance, the obscurity of smoke and the shining of a lamp, and hence Abram knew that light would at length emerge out of darkness. An analogy is always to be sought between signs and the things signified, that there may be a mutual correspondence between them; and since the symbol in itself is but a lifeless carcass, reference ought always to be made to the word which is annexed to it — here, by the word, liberty was promised to Abram's seed in the midst of servitude. The condition of the Church could not be painted more to the life, Calvin says, than when God causes a burning torch to proceed out of the smoke, in order that the darkness of afflictions may not overwhelm us, but that we may cherish a good hope of life even in death, because the Lord will at length shine upon us, if only we offer up ourselves in sacrifice to him. On the covenant itself he willingly admits that it was ratified by a solemn rite when the animals were divided into parts, and finds here a repetition which teaches what was the intent of the sacrifice already mentioned; and again he observes that the word is always to be joined with the symbols, lest our eyes be fed with empty and fruitless ceremonies. God has commanded animals to be offered to him, but he has shown their end and use by a covenant appended to them; and if the Lord feeds us by sacraments, we infer that they are the evidences of his grace and the tokens of those spiritual blessings which flow from it. Calvin adds that God then enumerates the nations whose land he was about to give to the sons of Abram, in order to confirm what he had said concerning a numerous offspring; for that was not to be a small band of men, but an immense multitude, for which the Lord assigns a habitation of such vast extent. He had before spoken only of the Amorites, among whom Abram then dwelt, but now, for the sake of amplifying his grace, he recounts all the others by name.

Ellicott identifies the vessel exactly: the word rendered smoking furnace really means the circular firepot which Orientals use in their houses to sit round for purposes of warmth. This one was wreathed in smoke, out of which shot a torch of flame; for not two symbols, but only one, passed between the divided carcases. Abram had probably passed between them immediately after arranging them, and now Jehovah does the same, fire being the recognised symbol of the Deity, as in the burning bush, the pillar of fire, and the lightnings on Mount Sinai.
