Of the covenant he notes that the Hebrew is, Jehovah cut a covenant: Abram had divided the slaughtered animals, and Jehovah, by passing between them, made the whole act his own. On the river of Egypt Ellicott is decided that the Nile is meant. In the Hebrew the winter torrent on the southern border of Simeon is always distinguished from the Nile, though the distinction is neglected in our version, and the word used here signifies a river that flows constantly; so Abram's posterity are to found a kingdom conterminous with the Nile and the Euphrates, that is, with Egypt and Babylonia. If these bounds are large and vague, we must also remember that they are limited by the names of the ten nations which follow: between the two rivers, the territory of these ten tribes alone is definitely bestowed upon Abram. Keil and Delitzsch describe the revelation as the making of a covenant, the Hebrew noun coming from a root meaning to cut — literally, the bond concluded by cutting up the sacrificial animals — and take the substance of the covenant to be embraced in the promise that God would give that land to the seed of Abram from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates. The river of Egypt, they agree, is the Nile and not the brook of Egypt, the boundary stream of the wilderness; according to the oratorical character of the promise, the two large rivers are mentioned as the boundaries within which the seed of Abram would possess the promised land, whose exact limits are more minutely described in the list of the tribes then in possession. Ten tribes are named, between the southern border of the land and the extreme north, to convey the impression of universality without exception.

19.pericope_label: The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Rephaims, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites

schools.summary: Clarke observes that ten nations are mentioned here, though afterwards reckoned but seven, and judges it probable that some of them which existed in Abram's time had been blended with others before the time of Moses, so that seven only out of the ten then remained. He then closes his comment on the chapter with three subjects which he says must be particularly interesting to the pious reader. The first is the condescension of God in revealing himself to mankind in a variety of ways, so as to render it absolutely evident that he had spoken, that he loved mankind, and that he had made every provision for their eternal welfare. So unequivocal were the discoveries which God made of himself that on the minds of those to whom they were made not one doubt was left, relative either to the truth of the subject or to the fact that God himself had made the discovery; and the subject of the discovery also sufficiently attested its truth to all future generations, for it concerned matters then in futurity, so distinctly marked, so positively promised, and so highly interesting, as to make them objects of attention, memory and desire till they came, and of gratitude, because of the permanent blessedness they communicated through all generations after the facts had taken place. The second is the way of salvation by faith in the promised Saviour, which now began to be explicitly declared. God gives the promise of salvation, and by means in which it was impossible, humanly speaking, that it should take place, teaching us that the whole work was spiritual, supernatural and divine, and that no human power could suffice to produce it. This Abram believed while he was yet uncircumcised, and this faith was accounted to him for righteousness; God thereby teaching that he would pardon, accept and receive into favour all who should believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and this very case has ever since been the standard of justification by faith, the experience of millions built on this foundation having sufficiently attested the truth and solidity of the ground on which it was built. The third is that the foundation of the doctrine itself is laid in the covenant made between God and Abram on behalf of all the families of the earth, and that this covenant is ratified by a sacrifice: by it man is bound to God, and God graciously binds himself to man. As the covenant referred to the incarnation of Christ, and Abram, both as to himself and as to his posterity, was to partake of its benefits by faith, hence faith and not works is the only condition on which God, through Christ, forgives sins and brings men to the promised spiritual inheritance. This covenant still stands open, Clarke says: all the successive generations of men are parties on the one side, and Jesus is at once the sacrifice and the Mediator of it; and since it stands open, every human soul must ratify it for himself, which no man does but he who, conscious of his guilt, accepts the sacrifice God has provided for him.

Gill reckons ten nations as occupying the land of Canaan at this time, whereas only seven are mentioned in the times of Moses and Joshua; the three that are wanting are not among those seven, and seem before those times to have become extinct, or to have been mixed with the other nations and to be no more distinct ones. He records the alternatives faithfully: Aben Ezra thinks these peoples had two names, while Jarchi, following the Jerusalem Talmud, interprets the three of the Edomites, Moabites and Ammonites, who shall be the inheritance of the children of Israel in future times. Some are of opinion, Gill adds, that the Midianites are meant by the Kenites, since Jethro, Moses's father-in-law, who was of Midian, is called the Kenite, as was also Heber, who was of the same race; there were Kenites near to the Amalekites in the times of Balaam, and who dwelt among them in the times of Saul, and there were also some of this name who descended from the father of the house of Rechab. Of the remaining tribes Gill gives chiefly their seats: the Hittites had their name from Heth, a son of Canaan, and dwelt about Hebron in the south of the land; the Amorites inhabited both on this and on the other side of Jordan; the Canaanites were a particular tribe or nation that bore the name of their great ancestor; the Girgashites are the same with the Gergesenes of the Gospel; and the Jebusites inhabited Jerusalem and about it, which was first called Jebus, from the founder of that nation.

Ellicott gives a short account of each of the three tribes that do not appear in the later lists. The Kenites he calls an Arab race, found both among the Amalekites in the south and among the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulon in the north, and even in Midian, since Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, is called a Kenite; Balaam speaks of them as being a powerful nation, and this wide dispersion of them into feeble remnants seems to him to show that they were a race of early settlers in Canaan who, like the Rephaim, had been overpowered and scattered by subsequent immigrants. They were uniformly friendly to Israel. Of the Kenizzites, the chief fact of importance connected with the race is that Caleb was one, who apparently with his clan joined the Israelites at the Exodus and was numbered with the tribe of Judah; Ellicott notes that the two English spellings of the name represent one Hebrew word, of which the first is the correct form. The Kadmonites, he says, may mean either an eastern or an ancient people, of whom we know nothing. For the rest of the nations named he refers the reader back to the earlier chapters of Genesis where each has already been described.
